questions.stem: A 57-year-old man was brought into the Emergency Department in a state of collapse. He was known to have end-stage liver disease. He had been bitten on the calf by a neighbor’s dog 5 days beforehand. He had not sought medical care immediately following the injury. On examination, he was profoundly unwell. His temperature was 35.2°C, blood pressure 72/42 mmHg, heart rate 142 beats/min, GCS 14/15. There were multiple purpuric lesions over his torso and limbs. The bite injury was scabbed but clean, with no pus or erythema. Investigations: Creatinine clearance 30 mL/min Lactate 4.6 mmol/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Capnocytophaga canimorsus Capnocytophaga canimorsus, commonly found in canine oral flora, can cause bacteremia and fulminant sepsis in humans, particularly those with asplenia or underlying liver disease. All of the organisms may be involved in bite injury infections, whether human, dog, or cat bite.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q28

questions.question: [image-based question: Staph streak on BAP shown with satelliting colonies]

parts.text: Name 3 genera of bacteria that have this characteristic.

questions.model_answer: Three genera exhibiting satellite phenomenon around a Staphylococcus streak on blood agar (due to Staph-produced NAD/hemin/X-V factors): (1) Haemophilus (e.g. H. influenzae, requires X and V factors). (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) actinomycetemcomitans. (3) Granulicatella / Abiotrophia (nutritionally variant streptococci, satellite due to pyridoxal requirement).

questions.question: Name the most likely pathogen for the following scenarios.

parts.text: AML patient with central venous catheter with sepsis and haemorrhagic bullous skin lesions. The aspirate is growing a GPR.
Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite.
CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea.

questions.model_answer: a) AML patient with CVC, sepsis, hemorrhagic bullous lesions, GPR growing on aspirate: most likely Bacillus cereus (or consider Clostridium species) - hemorrhagic bullae in neutropenic host with CVC and gram-positive rod strongly suggests Bacillus cereus bacteremia. b) Asplenic patient with sepsis after dog bite: Capnocytophaga canimorsus. c) Necrotizing scalp infection after swimming: Aeromonas hydrophila (freshwater exposure) - consider Vibrio vulnificus if saltwater exposure. d) CVID patient with chronic abdominal pain/diarrhea: Giardia lamblia.

questions.question: What is the most likely bug in the following scenarios?

parts.text: Scalp wound cellulitis from fresh water
CA patient with bullous skin lesions and Gram stain showing GPBs

cohort_answer.text: 1) Capnocytophaga canimorsus. 2) Aeromonas. Others: Burkholderia, Edwardsiella, Plesiomonas, Pseudomonas. Salt water: Vibrio, Shewanella, Erysipelothrix. 3) Giardia. 4) Clostridium septicum (w/o trauma), due to the malignancy

parts.text: Name two Gram negative bacteria that are seen in aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures and that grow on blood agar but not MacConkey

questions.question: Give diagnosis in each scenario:

parts.text: AML patient with line and fever and hemorrhagic bullae
Asplenic patient fever and hypotension after dog bite

questions.model_answer: a) AML patient with central line and fever with hemorrhagic bullae: ecthyma gangrenosum due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteremia. b) Freshwater injury of the head: Aeromonas hydrophila infection (also consider Naegleria fowleri if exposure via nasal water and meningoencephalitis symptoms). c) Asplenic patient with fever and hypotension after dog bite: Capnocytophaga canimorsus sepsis. d) [additional scenario not recalled - insufficient information to answer].

questions.question: Name the MOST likely infecting organism in the following scenarios:

parts.text: A patient on eculizumab with fever, nuchal rigidity and headache.
An immigrant person who is undergoing rituximab therapy
Therapy for multiple myeloma who presents with cough, dyspnea and a RLL infiltrate
A splenectomized person who had a dog bite 2 hours ago with bullae surrounding the wound

questions.model_answer:
a) Neisseria meningitidis.
b) Reactivation of chronic hepatitis B virus infection (rituximab-induced B-cell depletion carries a high risk of HBV reactivation, particularly relevant in an immigrant from an HBV-endemic region).
c) Streptococcus pneumoniae (multiple myeloma causes hypogammaglobulinemia, predisposing to infection with encapsulated organisms).
d) Capnocytophaga canimorsus (classically causes fulminant sepsis with bullous skin lesions after dog bites in asplenic patients).
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b-d draw on general ID knowledge of host-specific pathogen risk (rituximab/HBV reactivation, myeloma/hypogammaglobulinemia, asplenia/Capnocytophaga) beyond the Neisseria-specific Mandell chapter.
